name: Timofey and a flat tree
description: Little Timofey has a big tree — an undirected connected graph with n vertices and no simple cycles. He likes to walk along it. His tree is flat so when he walks along it he sees it entirely. Quite naturally, when he stands on a vertex, he sees the tree as a rooted tree with the root in this vertex. Timofey assumes that the more non-isomorphic subtrees are there in the tree, the more beautiful the tree is. A subtree of a vertex is a subgraph containing this vertex and all its descendants. You should tell Timofey the vertex in which he should stand to see the most beautiful rooted tree. Subtrees of vertices u and v are isomorphic if the number of children of u equals the number of children of v , and their children can be arranged in such a way that the subtree of the first son of u is isomorphic to the subtree of the first son of v , the subtree of the second son of u is isomorphic to the subtree of the second son of v , and so on. In particular, subtrees consisting of single vertex are isomorphic to each other.
input_specification: First line contains single integer n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ) — number of vertices in the tree. Each of the next n - 1 lines contains two integers u i and v i ( 1 ≤ u i , v i ≤ 10 5 , u i ≠ v i ), denoting the vertices the i -th edge connects. It is guaranteed that the given graph is a tree.
output_specification: Print single integer — the index of the vertex in which Timofey should stand. If there are many answers, you can print any of them.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 763D — Timofey and a flat tree [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
